newsitem.title: PARAGUAY: Paraguay police chiefs resign in stolen car scandal.
newsitem.headline: Paraguay police chiefs resign in stolen car scandal.

text.p: The entire top brass of the Paraguayan police force offered their resignation on Monday after a newspaper investigation revealed police involvement in trade in cars stolen in neighbouring Brazil.
"I have ordered the arrest of the officers involved and an investigation to find out who was responsible," President Juan Carlos Wasmosy told a news conference.
Hours earlier, police chief Mario Sapriza handed in his resignation along with the South American country's six regional commanders and 17 district commissioners.
Noticias newspaper carried out an investigation into the stolen car racket, with documents and photos proving police were in with thieves smuggling in vehicles stolen in Brazil.

Noticias journalists bought a stolen car in the city of Ciudad del Este, a notorious smuggling centre near the borders with Brazil and Argentina, and managed to bribe all the police checkpoints between there and the capital. They secretly took pictures of stolen car dealers and of police taking bribes.

"Our investigation has showed that there is structural police protection for criminal gangs, and that trafficking in cars is just one of their minor business activities," Noticias journalist Juan Salinas told Reuters.
Smuggling has long been rife in Paraguay, with about 500 stolen cars from Brazil estimated to cross the border every month, making up about 35 percent of vehicles on the road.
The security forces, who ran Paraguay under dictator Gen. Alfredo Stroessner until a coup in 1989, have frequently been accused of involvement in smuggling everything from whisky to cocaine.
Paraguay has about 12,000 police officers for a population of five million. Pay is low, at about $550 a month for lower ranking officers.
